models.best: Inferred from its principle that gifts create obligations to give and to return, members of a network carry each other's losses, so help after illness or a bad harvest comes through trust rather than premiums. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that gifts create obligations to give and to return, help is owed inside the network and not beyond it, so people outside a close circle of kin and allies have no claim on cover, and those inside may owe returns for years. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift; Sahlins, Stone Age Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a family farm balances its work against household needs, a household can spread illness or a poor harvest across the labour and stores of all its members. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production serves consumption, a household with few workers, or one struck by illness or a failed harvest, has no outside source of cover and must cut consumption or work harder to recover. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a central authority collects goods and stores them, the stores can cover a shortfall in one region from the surplus of the whole realm, so a bad harvest is spread across everyone who pays in. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the centre decides who receives from the stores, relief depends on rank and favour, so people who are not counted among its workers or officials may get little when stores run short, and relief is at the centre's discretion. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation; Polanyi, Arensberg and Pearson, Trade and Market in the Early Empires

models.best: Inferred from its principle that labour is extracted through the ownership of people, the owner bears the loss from an enslaved worker's illness or injury, which gives a direct financial reason to keep that labour fit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the enslaved are denied education and property, they hold no savings, fund or claim that could meet illness, injury or old age, so those risks fall on the person, and any relief depends on the owner's decision. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a lord gives land, protection and justice in return for labour and rent, a family's holding carries a standing claim on the manor's help in hard times. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour services and rents are owed to a lord for protection, cover depends on meeting those dues and on the lord's will, so a family unable to meet its services may lose both its holding and the protection that came with it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society; Capitulare de villis

models.best: Inferred from its principle that guilds regulate entry, training and prices within a trade, members of one trade share the same risks and can pool common funds for a master's illness or a journeyman's injury under their statutes. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that statutes control entry and training, workers outside the trade, and those who have not completed training, have no claim on the guild's common funds, so protection against misfortune depends on membership rather than on need. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Boileau, Le Livre des métiers; Epstein, Freedom and Growth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state aims for a trade surplus and colonies, it can back insurance for long voyages and colonial trade, spreading the risk of trade ventures across the state's own shipping. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that trade and colonies are regulated for the state's gain, insurance and risk-sharing follow those aims, so cover goes to privileged companies and favoured trades, while workers and households outside those trades have little comparable protection. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mun, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade; Heckscher, Mercantilism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the grain trade should be free, a poor harvest in one region can be met by grain from surplus regions, so a local shortfall is spread across the country. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a single tax on the rent of land funds the state, the core idea offers no route to cover for illness, accident or unemployment among people who do not work the land, and it places the cost of public funding on landowners alone. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Quesnay, Tableau économique; Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that competitive markets price goods and risks, insurers that compete for buyers have reason to match premiums to expected losses and to offer the cover that people choose to buy. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: US National Flood Insurance Program: the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968 created the federal programme because private insurers were largely unwilling to cover flood risk, given near-certain losses in some low-lying and coastal zones where homeowners would not pay premiums high enough, large regional catastrophe exposure and adverse selection. The reasons come from a search summary that does not tie each to a page. Source: Pew article on how 20th-century events shaped the National Flood Insurance Program (2016), with other US histories from 2005 to 2023 in the same search

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, premiums signal real risk, so buyers and insurers can see which losses cost most and act on that signal. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that state planning and credit expansion distort production, state guarantees and cheap credit can make risky building look safe, so the cost of disasters passes to the public rather than to the buyer who took the risk. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Menger, Grundsätze der Volkswirthschaftslehre; Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that deregulation, privatisation and a smaller state let insurers compete on price and product, so buyers can match cover to their own risks and pay only for what they need. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that deregulation, privatisation and a smaller state leave insurers free to refuse or price out high-risk buyers, so people exposed to illness, accident, job loss or disaster may go uncovered, with no public backstop to fall back on. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom; Harvey, A Brief History of Neoliberalism

models.best: US National Flood Insurance Program: the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968 created a federal programme because private insurers were largely unwilling to cover flood risk. The claim comes from a search summary that does not tie each point to a page.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that government spending and taxes steer demand, cover paid for from public budgets need not be priced to each person's exposure, so public cover can invite building and living in exposed places while taxpayers carry the losses. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Keynes, The General Theory; Beveridge, Social Insurance and Allied Services

models.best: Compulsory sickness funds in the Netherlands: a 1941 decree made cover compulsory for employees under a state-set income ceiling, and key features such as mutual risk equalisation partly survived later legislation. The later dates are not tied to a page, and historians dispute who shaped the decree, though not its date.
models.worst: Compulsory sickness funds in the Netherlands: cover was compulsory only for employees under a state-set income ceiling, so the self-employed and the elderly could enrol voluntarily and everyone else turned to private cover, and the later dates are not tied to a page. Source: Robert Vonk, article in the journal BMGN (2012); the 1964 and 2006 dates come from the same search summary and have no separate source

models.best: Union-run unemployment funds (the Ghent system): public money helps finance voluntary funds that unions run, and for Sweden one scholarly account says long-term strategy shaped the 1934 adoption. The claim is built from a search summary of several academic pages and is not tied to a page for each point.
models.worst: Union-run unemployment funds (the Ghent system): public money helps finance them, and in Sweden union density fell from 77% in 2006 to 71% in 2008 after a 2007 state funding cut. Researchers disagree on the funds' effect on union membership, so the fall does not show cause. The figures come from a search summary that does not tie each to a page, and they apply to Sweden alone. Source: A Cambridge-hosted academic article; Rasmussen and Pontusson (2017), a study cited in the results; a scholarly account of Sweden (years not shown)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state directs credit to chosen industries, public guarantees and insurance for export and investment risk can back those industries, so firms take risks they could not carry alone. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that firms are disciplined by performance, cover and guarantees that go to chosen industries leave firms outside the plan without support, and public cover can keep weak firms afloat when the model's discipline would let them fail. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle; Amsden, Asia's Next Giant

models.best: Inferred from its principle that land rent should fund public services, a levy on the value of land could pay for shared cover against disasters, so the rent of land pays for protection that everyone uses. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that land is taxed rather than labour and capital, a land tax would not reach illness, accident or unemployment directly, so cover for those risks would still depend on other funding and on the incomes of people who work. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities share work and goods among their members, illness, accident or old age is carried by the whole community, so no member is left to face such a loss alone. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that such communities are built by example and depend on members who join and stay, cover depends on how many join, how well the community is run and whether it lasts, so a failed community can leave its members with no cover at all. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Owen, A New View of Society; Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit and free contracts let members keep the full value of their work, a mutual pool can cover losses at cost, with no profit taken by an outside owner. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that rent on property is abolished and free contracts replace state and corporate control, a mutual pool has no outside backstop, so a loss larger than its members' contributions falls on members directly. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Japan's mutual life insurers: a Senshu University paper says mutual firms largely controlled life insurance for over 60 years, but that claim rests on one paper, neither its year nor its period is shown, and sources disagree on whether Japan's first life insurer was mutual. Friendly societies as approved societies in Britain ran day-to-day administration of the 1911 scheme, and the results cover that scheme only.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that members own the firm and share its surplus between users and workers, a surplus paid out as wages or dividends can leave thin reserves for a bad year, and a loss larger than the pooled money has no outside backstop. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers; Mondragón cooperatives

models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods are shared by need within federated communes, no one is left uncovered by illness, age or disability, because the commune gives each person what they need. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there are no wages and no state, cover rests only on what each commune holds and on members' willingness to share, so a disaster larger than local stocks has no wider backstop, and no one is obliged to contribute. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread

models.best: Union-run unemployment funds (the Ghent system): worker organisations rather than public bodies handle most jobless payouts. The claim is built from a search summary of several academic pages and is not tied to a page for each point.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that trade unions run industry directly through workers' organisations, their cover reaches members of organised trades and workplaces, while unorganised, casual and unemployed workers without a union card have no claim on that cover. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the French CGT; Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a national minimum of welfare is delivered by public enterprise and municipal bodies, every citizen can count on a floor of cover against illness, accident and unemployment, set and paid for democratically. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that change comes by democratic and gradual means, cover rises slowly through public enterprise and municipal bodies, so people whose needs grow faster than the minimum must wait or buy top-up cover, and the floor can stay low for a long time. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Fabian Essays in Socialism; Founding of the Fabian Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control of industry through guild-like councils, a trade's councils can run common cover for their members, with the state as one partner among several. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils of workers and consumers govern each industry, a trade's council can favour its own members, so cover for those outside the trade or without a council seat may be thin, and disputes among the partners can slow decisions about cover. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry

models.best: Inferred from its principle that central plans set output and investment, the state can pool a risk across the whole economy and provide cover through state enterprises to everyone who works for them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state mobilises labour for rapid industrialisation, cover can be tied to a worker's place in the plan, so workers outside state work have little claim on it, and a worker's illness or injury may be weighed against the plan's targets. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kornai, The Socialist System; First Five-Year Plan

models.best: Inferred from its principle that managers follow market prices under public ownership, cover can be priced from market signals, with a central board setting the rules and the investment that support it. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central board sets the rules and the investment, cover depends on that board's judgement of reserves and risk, and a public firm that prices cover by market signals can still have its premiums and reserves changed by rules set above it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Lange and Taylor, On the Economic Theory of Socialism; Yugoslav workers' self-management

models.best: Inferred from its principle that after classes disappear, distribution follows need, so illness, accident and old age are met from common provision, and no premiums or private cover are needed. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that distribution by need waits on the end of classes and the withering of the state, cover in the meantime depends on the transition, and the principle gives no account of how the sick and the unemployed are covered before that point. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership of key sectors sits alongside markets, state-owned insurers and banks can pool national risks, while market-priced cover serves the rest as reform proceeds gradually. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that price reform proceeds gradually under party direction, the scope and timing of cover can change at the centre, so households may face shifts in their cover for illness, old age and unemployment that they cannot plan for. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Naughton, The Chinese Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that councils of workers and consumers plan through repeated proposals, the risks of illness, accident and disaster can be shared by councils that agree cover within the same round of planning. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that neither markets nor central planners allocate, cover depends on repeated rounds of council proposals, so a sudden loss such as a disaster may wait for the next round, and the councils that must agree on cover can be slow to act on new risks. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward

models.best: Bismarck's compulsory accident insurance: after the 1884 statute made accident insurance mandatory for industrial firms, injured workers and their dependents received payouts. The claim rests on one study read only through search snippets.
models.worst: Bismarck's compulsory accident insurance: Guinnane and Streb attribute the shortfall to incentive design, since mutual insurance groups rated firms on pooled group experience, so individual firms had little financial reason to improve their own plants, and the scheme did not fully curb the growth of workplace accidents. The claim rests on one study read only through search snippets, which do not say who ran or financed the groups. Source: Guinnane and Streb, 'Incentives That (Could Have) Saved Lives', Journal of Economic History (2015); first circulated as a 2012 working paper

models.best: Takaful, the first Islamic mutual insurers, rests on a mutual guarantee among members with pooled money, and Malaysian insurers today ground their products in tabarru' (donation) and mudarabah (profit-sharing). The founding date and first company are disputed, and the Malaysian principles describe current practice, not early history.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that interest is prohibited and finance shares profit and risk, a mutual pool that runs short cannot borrow at interest to meet claims, so cover is limited to the money members have pooled, and a large loss can exceed it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System; Founding of the Mit Ghamr savings bank

models.best: Inferred from its principle that small, local and non-violent production serves well-being, neighbours who know one another can share losses directly, so help after illness or loss comes from people who can see the need. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production is small-scale and local, few risks are pooled across firms or regions, so a small community that suffers a shared loss, such as a fire or a failed harvest, has few outside sources of cover and relies on the goodwill of neighbours. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Buddhist Economics; Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful

models.best: Inferred from its principle that widespread private property and small enterprise give families their own means, a household with a holding or a small business has something to fall back on when illness or accident strikes, and subsidiarity keeps decisions near them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that small enterprise predominates, a small firm or a single household rarely has the reserves or numbers to spread a large loss, so cover for accident, illness or disaster may fall on families alone, while subsidiarity leaves larger risks with the smallest body competent to bear them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum; Belloc, The Servile State

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a social floor secures everyone within planetary limits, a guaranteed floor of cover can be funded from a stable economy, so no one falls below minimum protection against illness, accident or job loss. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no growth imperative, cover for rising claims, such as illness in old age or the cost of disasters, must be paid from a fixed economy, so benefits and reserves are limited and rising needs can strain the floor. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Daly, Steady-State Economics; Raworth, Doughnut Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every citizen receives an unconditional income, a loss of work or sudden illness does not leave anyone without a floor, and no one must prove need before receiving it. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the income is unconditional and the same for everyone, it does not match costs that differ from person to person, so large losses from illness, accident or disaster still need insurance on top, and the flat sum may fall short for people with high costs. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Paine, Agrarian Justice; Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government which issues its own currency can fund full employment, cover for unemployment and disaster can be paid as needed without relying on private insurers. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation, not debt, is the real limit, cover funded by spending can erode the value of benefits and savings when prices rise, so people holding cash or fixed claims bear the losses. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that communities who share a resource set and enforce their own rules, a shared pool of risk such as crop failure or flood can be governed by the people who bear it, with members monitoring one another. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that rules are nested in wider institutions, people outside the community have no claim on its pool, and a disaster larger than the shared resource can absorb may exceed the community's means without a wider institution. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons

compromise.summary: Compulsory core cover for illness, accident, unemployment and disaster, run by member-governed mutual bodies under public rules, with contributions set by income so that cover does not depend on employment; a public backstop for catastrophic risks; and voluntary private top-up cover above that.
compromise.details: Keeps: mutual ownership from Cooperative economy (Japan's mutual life insurers; Friendly societies as approved societies in Britain); union-run funds with public money from Nordic social democracy (Union-run unemployment funds (the Ghent system)); payouts to injured workers from Corporatism and fascist economics (Bismarck's compulsory accident insurance); mutual risk equalisation from Social market economy (Compulsory sickness funds in the Netherlands); the mutual guarantee from Islamic economics (Takaful, the first Islamic mutual insurers). Blocks: cover tied to employment, safeguarded by income-based contributions for every resident; group rating that dulls prevention, safeguarded by part of each premium set by the firm's record; uncovered catastrophic risk, safeguarded by a public backstop. Test: over several years, count residents without cover for illness, injury or job loss, compare firms' accident rates before and after rating, and check reserves each year. Source: Senshu University paper; Royal Commission report; Cambridge-hosted article; Guinnane and Streb (2015); Vonk (2012); Pew article (2016); Atlas takaful article.
